did_you_know.text: King Hezekiah, the officials, and the entire assembly decided to celebrate Passover in the second month rather than the first, as usual, after it became clear that the priests and the people were not yet sufficiently prepared.
Hezekiah and his officials sent messengers throughout Israel—from Beersheba to Dan—to invite the people to come to Jerusalem and celebrate Passover to the LORD.
The king’s letters called on the Israelites to return to the LORD, in the hope that the LORD would have mercy on them and that their relatives who had been taken captive would return to the land.
The messengers were met with ridicule and scorn in the territories of Ephraim, Manasseh, and Zebulun, but some people from Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun humbled themselves and came to Jerusalem.
Before celebrating Passover, the people of Jerusalem removed the altars and incense altars and threw them into the Kidron Valley as part of the city’s purification.

Many of those who came, especially from Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar, and Zebulun, had not purified themselves properly. Hezekiah prayed that the LORD would forgive them because their hearts were set on seeking him.
The LORD heard Hezekiah’s prayer and healed the people, according to the account in the chapter.
The celebrants decided to continue the festival for another seven days, so they celebrated for a total of fourteen days with joy.
Hezekiah contributed a thousand bulls and seven thousand sheep and goats for the assembly, and the officials contributed another thousand bulls and ten thousand sheep and goats.
The chapter describes the joy in Jerusalem as exceptionally great, saying that there had been nothing like it in the city since the days of Solomon son of David, king of Israel.
